title: Ezekiel 36:1–15
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to prophesy to the mountains of Israel, the same mountains that heard judgment in chapter 6. The enemy, including Edom (36:5), has mocked them and claimed the ancient high places as a possession, and the land has become a byword among the nations (36:2–7). Now the Lord GOD swears that the nations will bear their own shame, while the mountains of Israel will put out branches and fruit for his returning people (36:8–12). The land once spoken of as devouring its inhabitants (compare Numbers 13:32) will no longer bereave its nation (36:13–15). The repeated refrain “you will know that I am the LORD” continues. Both traditions read the unit as the LORD reversing judgment into restoration, and they see the land’s renewal as tied to the return of his people.

verses.text: You, son of man, prophesy to the mountains of Israel, and say, “You mountains of Israel, hear the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ezekiel to prophesy to the mountains of Israel, telling them to hear the LORD’s word. Arminian readers note the reversal: the mountains that received judgment in chapter 6 now receive a word of hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s faithfulness to the land he gave, even after judgment. Both traditions read the address to the mountains as personification, setting the land itself before the LORD as a hearer of his promise.

verses.text: The Lord GOD says: ‘Because the enemy has said against you, “Aha!” and, “The ancient high places are ours in possession!” ’
verses.arminianNotes: The enemy said, Aha, and claimed the ancient high places as their possession. Arminian readers see the enemy’s taunt as presumption, assuming Israel’s land was now free for the taking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the claim as an affront to the LORD, whose land it was. Shared ground: both traditions read the quoted words as the provocation to which the LORD now responds.

verses.text: therefore prophesy, and say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Because, even because they have made you desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that you might be a possession to the residue of the nations, and you are taken up in the lips of talkers, and the evil report of the people;”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD notes that the mountains have been made desolate, swallowed up, and made the talk of the nations. Arminian readers see the shame Israel’s land has borne, mocked by surrounding peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD taking up the cause of his land, which has become a byword. Both traditions read the verse as describing humiliation that the LORD will soon reverse, as the following verses show.

verses.text: therefore, you mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD: The Lord GOD says to the mountains and to the hills, to the watercourses and to the valleys, to the desolate wastes and to the cities that are forsaken, which have become a prey and derision to the residue of the nations that are all around;
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD addresses mountains, hills, watercourses, valleys, wastes, and forsaken cities that became prey and derision. Arminian readers see every part of the land included in the coming word of hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of 6:3, where the same list introduced judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the repetition as deliberate, showing that the places once judged are now the places addressed with promise.

verses.text: therefore the Lord GOD says: “Surely in the fire of my jealousy I have spoken against the residue of the nations, and against all Edom, that have appointed my land to themselves for a possession with the joy of all their heart, with despite of soul, to cast it out for a prey.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks in the fire of his jealousy against the nations and all Edom, who claimed his land with joy and contempt. Arminian readers see God’s jealousy as protective love for his people and land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s zeal for his own honor and possession. Both traditions read jealousy here as God’s rightful claim, not petty envy, and they connect the verse to chapter 35’s oracle against Edom.

verses.text: Therefore prophesy concerning the land of Israel, and tell the mountains, the hills, the watercourses and the valleys, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I have spoken in my jealousy and in my wrath, because you have borne the shame of the nations.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD speaks in jealousy and wrath because the land has borne the nations’ shame. Arminian readers see God identifying with his suffering land and people, taking their reproach as his concern.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD acting to vindicate what belongs to him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God turning his wrath from Israel toward those who mocked Israel’s ruin.

verses.text: Therefore the Lord GOD says: “I have sworn, ‘Surely the nations that are around you will bear their shame.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD swears that the surrounding nations will bear their own shame. Arminian readers see a reversal of roles, as those who shamed Israel now face shame themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath as guaranteeing that God’s justice will reach the nations. Both traditions read the verse as part of the larger pattern of reversal in these chapters, with judgment and restoration exchanged.

verses.text: “ ‘ “But you, mountains of Israel, you shall shoot out your branches and yield your fruit to my people Israel; for they are at hand to come.
verses.arminianNotes: The mountains of Israel will shoot out branches and fruit for the LORD’s people, who are about to come. Arminian readers see the land preparing to welcome its people home, a hopeful image after exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise of return as certain, since the LORD speaks of it as near. Shared ground: both traditions read the fruitful mountains as a sign of renewed blessing, the reverse of the desolation in chapter 6.

verses.text: For, behold, I am for you, and I will come to you, and you will be tilled and sown.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, I am for you, and the land will be tilled and sown. Arminian readers note the striking contrast with I am against you in earlier oracles, showing God’s turn toward mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s favor as the foundation of the land’s renewal. Both traditions read I am for you as a central word of the chapter, marking the shift from judgment to restoration.

verses.text: I will multiply men on you, all the house of Israel, even all of it. The cities will be inhabited and the waste places will be built.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will multiply people on the land, all the house of Israel, and the cities will be rebuilt. Arminian readers see the promise embracing the whole people, not only one tribe or group.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase all of it as stressing the completeness of God’s restoring work. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a promise of repopulation and rebuilding, hope for exiles far from home.

verses.text: I will multiply man and animal on you. They will increase and be fruitful. I will cause you to be inhabited as you were before, and you will do better than at your beginnings. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will multiply people and animals, and the land will do better than at its beginnings. Arminian readers see blessing that surpasses the past, a generous promise beyond mere recovery.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language of increase and fruitfulness recalling creation and covenant blessing. Both traditions read the verse as abundant restoration, ending with the refrain that they will know the LORD.

verses.text: Yes, I will cause men to walk on you, even my people Israel. They will possess you, and you will be their inheritance, and you will never again bereave them of their children.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will cause his people to walk on the land and possess it, and it will never again bereave them of children. Arminian readers see the land becoming a place of life rather than loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the land restored as Israel’s inheritance by God’s gift. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise of no more bereavement as a tender reversal of the losses of war and exile.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “Because they say to you, ‘You are a devourer of men, and have been a bereaver of your nation;’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD notes that people say the land devours men and bereaves its nation. Arminian readers see an echo of the spies’ report in Numbers 13:32 by reference, a reputation the land had carried.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the saying as reflecting the land’s history of famine, war, and judgment. Both traditions read the verse as introducing the LORD’s promise to remove that reproach.

verses.text: therefore you shall devour men no more, and not bereave your nation any more,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the land will no longer devour people or bereave its nation. Arminian readers see the reversal of the land’s sad reputation through God’s renewing work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s word as decisive, overturning what had seemed the land’s fixed character. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise as part of the restoration that removes shame from Israel.

verses.text: “I won’t let you hear the shame of the nations any more. You won’t bear the reproach of the peoples any more, and you won’t cause your nation to stumble any more,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The land will no longer hear the taunts of the nations, bear the peoples’ reproach, or make its nation stumble. Arminian readers connect this freedom from reproach with the renewed relationship the chapter goes on to promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise as God’s gift, securing the land against future reproach. Both traditions read the verse as closing the unit with a firm assurance spoken by the Lord GOD.
